title: After Uhud — The Years of Testing
era: Two Years of Treachery and Repair
teaser: Uhud cost them their reputation. What followed was two years of ambush, betrayal, and quiet repair.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: What one defeat costs a young state
layers.content:
Uhud did not destroy Madinah. It damaged something harder to repair — the belief among the tribes that the Muslims could not be beaten. Within weeks the Jews, the hypocrites and the Bedouins were declaring their hostility openly, and the trouble came from four directions at once.

Banu Asad bin Khuzaymah began preparing a raid on Madinah before two months had passed. In Safar of 4 AH the tribes of Adi and Qarah conspired against the Muslims and ten Companions were killed. Banu Amir plotted in the same month, and seventy Companions died at the Well of Ma'unah. Banu Nadir, inside Madinah itself, moved from announcing their enmity to an attempt on the Prophet's life in Rabi'ul-Awwal of 4 AH. By Jumada al-Awwal, Banu Ghatafan were preparing to attack the town.

His first answer had been the march to Hamra'ul-Asad, the morning after the battle. What followed was a sequence of dispatched expeditions, each one aimed at a specific gathering threat before it could arrive.

The first went out on the 1st of Muharram, 4 AH. Word reached Madinah that Talhah and Salamah, the sons of Khuwaylid, were raising volunteers among Banu Asad. The Prophet ﷺ sent a hundred and fifty men of the Helpers and Emigrants under Abu Salamah. They reached Banu Asad in their own country, caught them unprepared, scattered them and took their cattle. There was no battle. On the way home Abu Salamah's wound from Uhud became inflamed, and he died of it.

That is the shape of these two years. Not one great confrontation, but a long run of small journeys, some of which ended in a captured herd and some of which ended in nobody coming back.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Two Invitations
layers.subtitle: Both requests for teachers were traps
layers.content:
In Safar of 4 AH a delegation from Adi and Qarah came to Madinah and asked for men who could teach them the religion. They said some among them were already Muslims. He sent six Companions; another version says ten. The leader was Marthad bin Abi Marthad al-Ghanawi, though al-Bukhari names Asim bin Thabit — the grandfather of Asim bin Umar bin al-Khattab.

At a place called Ar-Raji', between Rabigh and Jeddah, a hundred archers of Banu Lihyan surrounded them. The Companions took high ground. The Bedouins offered a pledge that they would not be killed. Asim refused to come down and fought until he and six others were dead. Three were left: Khubayb bin Adi, Zayd bin ad-Dathinah, and one more. The pledge was offered again and this time accepted; when they descended they were bound. The third man denounced the treachery and fought, and was killed. The other two had killed notables of Quraysh at Badr, so they were taken to Makkah and sold there.

The second invitation was worse. Abu Bara' Amir bin Malik, called the Spear Player, came to Madinah and would neither accept Islam nor refuse it. Send men to the people of Najd, he said, and I expect they will accept. The Prophet ﷺ answered that he feared the people of Najd would kill them. I will protect them, Abu Bara' said.

Ibn Ishaq puts the party at forty; the Sahih says seventy, and al-Mubarakpuri holds that to be correct. They were the best of the reciters. On the road they gathered firewood by day and sold it to buy food for the destitute men who slept in the mosque, and studied the Qur'an at night. At the Well of Ma'unah they sent the Prophet's letter ahead with Haram bin Milhan. Amir bin at-Tufayl did not read it. He had Haram speared in the back. Seeing his own blood, Haram said: Allahu Akbar — by the Lord of the Ka'bah, I have won.

Banu Amir refused to attack men under Abu Bara's protection. Banu Sulaim did not refuse. Ri'l, Dhakwan and Usayyah answered the call, and the party was killed to the last man but one.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the expeditions of Ar-Raji' and the Well of Ma'unah
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: Khubayb at At-Tan'im
layers.subtitle: The question Abu Sufyan should not have asked
layers.content:
Khubayb was held in Makkah while they argued over him, and the decision was crucifixion. They took him out of the sanctuary to At-Tan'im.

He asked for a delay to pray two units of prayer. When he had finished he turned to the men waiting to kill him and said: had I not feared you would think I was afraid of death, I would have prayed longer. He was the first to set that practice: two rak'ahs before execution. Then he said: Lord, count them one by one, and destroy them to the last.

He recited verses of his own. The confederates have gathered their tribes around me and brought their women and children, and I am bound to a tall trunk. They gave me the choice of disbelief, and death is preferable. By Allah, I do not care, if I die a Muslim, on which side I fall.

Then Abu Sufyan asked him a question. Do you not wish that Muhammad were here in your place, so we might cut off his head and you could go home? Khubayb answered: by Allah, I do not wish that Muhammad were where I am standing. I would not wish a thorn to hurt him, even to be returned to my family.

Uqbah bin al-Harith, whose father Khubayb had killed, carried out the crucifixion. A guard was set on the body; Amr bin Umayyah ad-Damri took it down in the dark and buried it. Shortly before, he had been seen eating a bunch of grapes, when there was not a date to be had in Makkah.

Quraysh sent a man to take a piece of Asim bin Thabit's body. He could not reach it: a swarm of hornets covered it. Asim had pledged to his Lord that no polytheist would ever handle him. When Umar bin al-Khattab heard, he said: Allah protects His believing servant after death as He does in life.

For thirty days, in every Fajr prayer, the Prophet ﷺ invoked Allah against Ri'l, Dhakwan, Lihyan and Usayyah. Anas reported it. Then a verse came down which the Companions recited for a time before it was abrogated — inform our people that we have met our Lord, He is pleased with us and He has made us pleased — and he stopped.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the killing of Khubayb bin Adi; and narrated by Anas, the thirty days of supplication after Ma'unah
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Expulsion and Surah al-Hashr
layers.subtitle: Six hundred camels left Madinah loaded
layers.content:
The chain that led to Banu Nadir began with a mistake. Amr bin Umayyah, coming home from Ma'unah, killed two sleeping men of Bani Kilab, not knowing they had been granted protection. The Prophet ﷺ said: you have killed two men, and their blood money is a debt I must discharge. The treaty obliged Banu Nadir to contribute a share.

He went with Abu Bakr, Umar and Ali. They agreed to pay, and asked him to wait beside one of their walls. In the meeting that followed, Amr bin Jahsh offered to climb up and drop a stone on his head. Sallam bin Mishkam warned that Allah would disclose it and that it broke the pact. Jibreel came down with the plot, and he left.

Muhammad bin Maslamah carried the ultimatum: leave within ten days. Abdullah bin Ubai told them to stay and promised two thousand men, plus Quraydhah and Ghatafan. «لَئِنْ أُخْرِجْتُمْ لَنَخْرُجَنَّ مَعَكُمْ» — 'If you are expelled, we too will go out with you.' (59:11) Huyay bin Akhtab sent back: we will not leave our houses; do as you like.

The siege lasted six nights, or fifteen by another report. The Muslims were ordered to cut and burn the palm groves the defenders sheltered behind: «مَا قَطَعْتُمْ مِنْ لِينَةٍ أَوْ تَرَكْتُمُوهَا قَائِمَةً عَلَى أُصُولِهَا فَبِإِذْنِ اللهِ» — 'Whatever palm trees you cut or left standing on their roots was by the permission of Allah.' (59:5) Quraydhah stayed neutral. Ibn Ubai and Ghatafan sent nobody; of them the Sura says they were like Satan, who tells a man to disbelieve and then says: I am free of you. (59:16)

Banu Nadir asked to leave. They were allowed all their camels could carry except weapons, and took even the door frames and roof beams. Six hundred loaded camels went out, to Khaybar and to Syria. This was Rabi'ul-Awwal 4 AH, August 625 CE. Almost the whole of Surah al-Hashr is about it: «هُوَ الَّذِي أَخْرَجَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ مِنْ دِيَارِهِمْ» — 'It is He who drove out the disbelievers among the People of the Book from their homes.' (59:2)
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: The battle that nobody came to fight
layers.content:
Banu Nadir's wealth was taken without fighting, so it was not divided as battlefield spoils. It went at the Prophet's discretion to the early Emigrants and to two poor Helpers, Abu Dujanah and Sahl bin Hunayf, with a portion for his family's year and the rest spent on arming the men. Fifty suits of armour, fifty helmets and three hundred and forty swords came with it. In the same Sura, Allah praised the Helpers who «وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَى أَنْفُسِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ» — 'give others preference over themselves, even when they are in need.' (59:9)

At Uhud, Abu Sufyan had called out an appointment to meet again at Badr a year later. In Sha'ban of 4 AH the Prophet ﷺ went out to keep it with fifteen hundred fighters and ten horsemen, Ali carrying the standard. Abu Sufyan set out with two thousand foot and fifty cavalry, got as far as Majannah near Makkah, and lost his nerve. He told Quraysh nothing would help them but a fruitful year, that this one looked rainless, and that he was going home. They obeyed at once.

The Muslims waited at Badr eight days, traded at a profit and went home. The expedition carries several names — Badr the Appointment, the Second Badr, the Minor Badr — and no fighting occurred at any of them.

At the end of Rabi'ul-Awwal in 5 AH, news came that tribes near Dumatul-Jandal, on the Syrian frontier, were robbing caravans and gathering against Madinah. He marched a thousand men fifteen days north, moving by night and hiding by day. The enemy had gone. He stayed five days, sent out patrols, found nobody, and on the way back made peace with Uyaynah bin Hisn.

Carry this. The two years after Uhud contain no famous victory. They contain a man tied to a post at At-Tan'im refusing to wish harm on the Prophet ﷺ to save his own life, and a rival army turning back rather than face the people he belonged to. Reputation was not recovered by winning a battle. It was recovered by showing up to one, repeatedly, until the other side stopped coming.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 59:9 — 'and they give others preference over themselves, even when they are in need'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: How many Companions were sent to teach the tribes of Adi and Qarah, the party ambushed at Ar-Raji'?

options.text: Seventy, all of them reciters of the Qur'an
Six in one version, ten in another
One hundred and fifty
Three, sent secretly

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Raji' Mobilization
quiz.scholar_reflection: The sources differ on the number and on who led them: Marthad bin Abi Marthad al-Ghanawi in one account, Asim bin Thabit in al-Bukhari's. What they agree on is that a hundred archers met a handful of teachers.

quiz.prompt: What did Khubayb bin Adi ask for before his crucifixion, setting a precedent afterwards followed?

options.text: Water to drink
A message carried to his family
A delay to pray two units of prayer
To be killed by the sword instead

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He cut the prayer short deliberately, so his executioners would not mistake length for fear. He was the first to establish two rak'ahs before execution.

quiz.prompt: How many Companions were killed at the Well of Ma'unah?

options.text: Ten
Forty according to Ibn Ishaq, seventy according to the Sahih — which al-Mubarakpuri holds to be correct
Exactly three hundred
None — the party returned safely

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Tragedy at the Well of Ma'unah
quiz.scholar_reflection: One man survived, Ka'b bin Zayd, carried out wounded from among the dead. He was killed two years later at the Trench.

quiz.prompt: Why did the Prophet ﷺ go to Banu Nadir shortly before their expulsion?

options.text: To demand they leave Madinah
To ask their share of blood money owed under the treaty, for two men killed in error
To buy weapons from them
To invite them to a public debate

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Invasion of Bani An-Nadeer
quiz.scholar_reflection: He came to them on the strength of the treaty, asking them to honour a clause they had signed. While he sat waiting by their wall, they discussed dropping a stone on his head.

quiz.prompt: What happened at the Second Badr, the appointment Abu Sufyan had called out at Uhud?

options.text: A battle larger than the first Badr
Abu Sufyan turned back, citing a rainless year; the Muslims waited eight days, traded, and went home
The Muslims failed to arrive
A truce was signed on the battlefield

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Second Battle of Badr
quiz.scholar_reflection: He came out with two thousand men and fifty horses, reached Majannah, and told his people the year looked dry. They agreed at once. That was the whole battle.

quiz.prompt: Abu Sufyan asked Khubayb whether he would rather Muhammad ﷺ were on the post in his place. Khubayb said he would not wish a thorn to hurt him, even to go home. What is that?

options.text: Love that has stopped calculating its own cost
Refusal to give an enemy the satisfaction of a crack
A man who had already accepted he was going to die
Certainty about what he was dying for, held all the way down

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari — the account of Khubayb bin Adi at At-Tan'im
quiz.scholar_reflection: The question was designed to find a limit. Bound to a trunk, hours from death, with his family offered back to him, he was asked to name a price. He did not have one.

quiz.prompt: The seventy sent to Najd gathered and sold firewood on the road so they could feed the homeless men sleeping in the mosque, and studied Qur'an at night. Then they were killed in an ambush. How do you sit with that?

options.text: It is unbearable, and the sources do not try to soften it
Their worth is in what they were doing, not in how it ended
The Prophet ﷺ warned that Najd would kill them and was overruled by a guarantee
That the best of them were sent is exactly why the loss mattered so much

quiz.slider_label: A senseless loss — A completed life
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the reciters sent to the Well of Ma'unah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He said plainly: I am afraid the people of Najd will kill them. He sent them because a protector guaranteed them. The guarantee held for the tribe that gave it, and for nobody else.

quiz.prompt: Amr bin Umayyah killed two sleeping men in revenge for his companions, not knowing they were under the Prophet's protection. The Prophet ﷺ said their blood money was a debt he himself must pay. What does that establish?

options.text: Grief does not license killing, and the community absorbs the cost of its member's error
A guarantee of protection means nothing unless it is honoured after it is broken
He could have disowned the act and did not
Leadership means paying for damage you did not cause

quiz.slider_label: The individual answers — The community answers
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — 'their blood money shall be a debt I have to discharge'
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not excuse it on the grounds of provocation, and he did not abandon the man who did it. He went out and collected the money.

quiz.prompt: For thirty days he invoked Allah against the tribes who had killed his Companions. Then a revelation came about the dead, and he stopped. What changed?

options.text: He had learned the dead were content, which removed the grievance
Thirty days of anger, honestly expressed, then closed — not suppressed and not permanent
Cursing was for as long as he had no other answer
The revelation redirected his attention from the killers to the killed

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Anas — the thirty days of supplication after the Well of Ma'unah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He named four tribes every dawn for a month. That is a long time to be angry out loud, and it stopped the moment he was told his people had met their Lord and were pleased.

quiz.prompt: Abu Sufyan had publicly set the appointment at Badr, then talked his own army out of coming. The Muslims waited, traded and went home, and their standing across Arabia rose. What do you take from that?

options.text: Turning up is often the whole of it
Reputation is repaired by consistency, not by a single spectacular result
The side that avoids the meeting has already conceded something
They went out to fight and got a market instead, and took that too

quiz.slider_label: Won by fighting — Won by showing up
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Second Battle of Badr
quiz.scholar_reflection: Nothing happened at the Second Badr, and Arabia drew a conclusion from it anyway. Sometimes the record of who arrived is the whole argument.
